en: Appendix 1:
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
A Concise Commentary on the Subjects Included within the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*.
The eight categories beginning with omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*),
as well as the seventy categories beginning with the production of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*), constitute the subject matter of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*.
Their essential nature is here presented in brief.
The eight categories are:
the knowledge of all aspects,
the knowledge of the paths, and so forth.
Omniscience (knowledge of things),
the complete awakening to all aspects,
and the culminating clear realization.
The gradual realization (*ānupūrvikābhisamaya*), the realization in a single moment (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodha*),
and the *dharmakāya*— these eight topics are presented in two verses of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* as follows:
The perfection of wisdom is proclaimed by means of eight categories:
omniscience in all its aspects, knowledge of the paths, and then omniscience.
Complete awakening in all its aspects, the culminating stage, the serial [awakening],
the momentary complete awakening, and the dharma-body— these are the eightfold [stages].

1. *Sarvākārajñatā* (a): The definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is that ultimate knowledge which, in a single moment, directly realizes the aspects of all objects of knowledge exactly as they are; this is the definition of *sarvākārajñatā*.
(kha) The divisions: "knowledge of the extent" (yāvajjñāna) and "knowledge of the manner" (yathāvajjñāna) are the two divisions of the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).
That wisdom which knows all modes without exception is "knowledge of the extent."
That which knows the intrinsic nature of things exactly as they are is "knowledge of reality" (*yathāvajjñāna*).

Alternatively, there is one division: the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñāna*), which directly realizes all modes of the causes such as the production of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*) and their untainted fruits (*anāsravaphala*) without exception.
There is a second division: the twenty-two types of untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) that arise on the stage of a Buddha (*buddhabhūmi*).
(ga) Limit: Omniscience in all its aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) exists exclusively on the level of a Buddha;
[the second is] knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*).
(a) Definition:

The definition of the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñatā*) is the state of being the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the noble Mahāyāna, characterized by being apprehended by a wisdom that directly realizes the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) of the three paths. (b) Classification: [The classification follows.]

It has four divisions, namely: the knowledge of the path of the śrāvakas, the knowledge of the path of the pratyekabuddhas, [the knowledge of the path of the bodhisattvas, and the knowledge of all paths].
The knowledge of the path of the Mahāyāna,
and the knowledge of all wisdom and skillful means residing in the mental continuum of the noble ones of the Mahāyāna; thus [is] the limit.
Starting from the Mahāyāna path of seeing up to the stage of Buddhahood, this constitutes the limit of the knowledge of paths (*mārgajñatā*).
3. The characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*, i.e., *vastujñatā*). (a) [The characteristic of the basis.]

The definition of the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñatā*) is the gnosis abiding in the continuum of an Ārya of the Hīnayāna lineage, which has been acquired through a wisdom that directly realizes the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) as it pertains to all phenomena.

That gnosis abiding in the continuum of an Ārya of the Hīnayāna lineage directly realizes emptiness, which is a synonym for the selflessness of persons; because it is acquired by means of that [wisdom], the qualification "of the Hīnayāna lineage" is applied to the definition of the knowledge of the path.

(kha) The division consists of two types of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*): that which is distant from and that which is not distant from the Mother of the Victors (*jinajananī*) as its fruit. (ga) The limit (*avadhi*).
Beginning from the path of seeing of the Śrāvakas and extending up to the stage of a Buddha, this constitutes the limit of omniscience.
4. The Manifest Realization of All Aspects (Sarvākārābhisambodha): (a) Its Characteristics.

The definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is the realization of all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*), which consists in the attainment of the union with sentient beings through the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya-prajñā*) regarding the aspects of the three types of omniscience.
(kha) Its classification (*bheda*) by way of its essential nature (*svarūpa*) consists of twenty applications (*prayoga*).

The modes of application (*satvayoga*) that bring about the realization of the one hundred and seventy-three aspects (*ākāra*) connected with the three types of omniscience constitute the one hundred and seventy-three divisions of this complete awakening to all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*). These modes of application are as follows: [the list follows].
the perfection of the path,
the bodhisattva path,
and the practice of the Mahāyāna;
"Armed practice"—these are synonyms.
(ga) The limit: beginning from the Mahāyāna path of equipment up to the state of the Bodhisattva abiding in the final moment, this constitutes the boundary for the realization of all aspects.
5. The Culminating Clear Realization (mūrdhābhisamaya):

(a) Its characteristic consists of the three aspects of the three types of omniscience, which have been grasped by means of the wisdom consisting of cultivation that has emptiness as its object, and which are established through that very vision.

The definition of the *mūrdhābhisamaya* (culminating clear realization) is the yoga of existence (*sattvayoga*) at the ultimate limit of cultivation, which is the "summit application" (*mūrdhaprayoga*).

Since the applications acquired by a bodhisattva through wisdom consisting of hearing are also subsumed within this very [realization], the qualification is established from that perspective within the definition. (b) The classification.
In brief, there is the summit application belonging to the path of preparation, the summit application belonging to the path of seeing,
and the summit application belonging to the path of cultivation.
There are four divisions: the immediate (*ānantarya*) and the summit (*mūrdhan*) applications.

Alternatively, there are the four applications of the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) known as heat (*ūṣman*), summit (*mūrdhan*), patience (*kṣānti*), and the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*);

and the three applications of the paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)—namely, the immediate, the summit, and the application [of the path of seeing]—thus making seven summit applications in total.
In detail, however, it should be understood that there are one hundred and seventy-three applications of the summit (*mūrdhaprayoga*).

(ga) Regarding the limit: its boundary extends from the application of the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) stage on the path of application (*prayogamārga*) of the Mahāyāna up to the state of the Bodhisattva abiding in the final moment.
6. Gradual Realization (*ānupūrvikābhisamaya*).
(a) Definition:

The definition is that the gradual application is the cultivation of the yoga of sentient beings, established as a process of meditative cultivation for the sake of stabilizing the aspects of the three types of omniscience.
(kha) Classification: There are thirteen classifications of this sequential clear realization. (ga) Limitation:
Beginning from the Mahāyāna path of equipment (*sambhāramārga*) and extending back to the stage prior to the state of a bodhisattva abiding in the final moment, this constitutes its limit.
7. *Ekakṣaṇābhisambodha* (Enlightenment in a Single Moment):

The definition is that the ultimate mental application (*sattvayoga*) produced through gradual cultivation for the sake of thoroughly mastering the aspects of the three types of omniscience is the definition of enlightenment in a single moment.
(kha) Differentiation:
through its exclusion [from others], it has four divisions. (ga) Limitation.
This application occurs exclusively during the stage of the bodhisattva in his final existence.
8. The Dharmakāya (a) its characteristics.
The definition [of the Dharmakāya] is: the fruit produced by the power of the intensification of the cultivation of the aspects of the three types of omniscience, or the ultimate untainted qualities;
its classification is the Svabhāvakāya.
Its four divisions are the wisdom-dharmakāya, the enjoyment-body (sāmbhogikakāya), and the emanation-body (nairmāṇikakāya).
(ga) The limit: this *dharmakāya* exists exclusively on the stage of a Buddha.
There are seventy topics.
The thirty factors that characterize the three types of omniscience, the thirty-six factors that characterize the four applications,
and the four factors that characterize the dharma-body— these seventy topics are analyzed and explained individually according to these three divisions.

1. The thirty dharmas that characterize the three types of omniscience (*trisarvajñatā*) consist of thirty dharmas that characterize the three types of omniscience: ten that awaken one to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), eleven that awaken one to the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and nine that awaken one to the knowledge of all [phenomena] (*sarvajñatā*); thus, there are thirty.

(a) There are ten factors that characterize the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*): therein, 1. the generation of the mind of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyānacittotpāda*), 2. instruction (*avavāda*), and 3. the factors of penetration (*nirvedhāṅga*).
4. The basis for the practice of the Mahāyāna; 5. The objective support for the practice of the Mahāyāna;
6. The summary of the practice of the Mahāyāna.
7. The practice of armor, 8. the practice of setting out, 9. the practice of equipment.

10. Regarding the practice of departure (*niryāṇapratipatti*), ten factors that characterize the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are demonstrated in two verses of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, as follows:
"The production of the thought [of awakening], the instruction, and the fourfold limb of penetration."
And the basis for practice has the nature of the dharmadhātu.
The object, the aim, the acts of donning armor and setting forth, the accumulations together with the departure— these constitute the omniscience of all aspects belonging to the Sage.
1. The production of the thought [of awakening] is its characteristic; its classification and its object are [as follows].
The limit and so forth—these four are to be known.
All of this has been explained in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* by means of three verses. For instance:
"The production of the thought [of awakening] is the desire for perfect enlightenment for the sake of others."
And that [classification] is stated both in brief and in detail, according to the sūtras.
By means of the earth, gold, the moon, and fire; by treasures, mines of jewels, and oceans;
by diamonds, mountains, medicinal herbs, and friends; by wish-fulfilling gems, the sun, and songs;
and by kings, treasuries, great highways, vehicles, and flowing waters.
And that [joy] is of twenty-two kinds, like clouds over the river of Ānanda’s speech.
(a) The definition:

The generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*) is a distinguished mental consciousness belonging to the Mahāyāna, which is brought forth by a desire based on its own cause for the sake of others, and is associated with the aspiration for enlightenment; this is its definition.
(b) The object of focus (*ālambana*).

The generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*) proceeds by taking as its object both one's own welfare, which is enlightenment, and the welfare of others, which is the *nirvāṇa* residing within the continuums of others.

(ga) As for its divisions: in terms of its essential nature, there are two types of the generation of the mind, namely, that which has the nature of the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhipraṇidhi*) and that which has the nature of the setting out toward enlightenment (*bodhiprasthāna*).
Through the view associated with mental factors, there are twenty-two distinctions of the arising of the mind, namely:
1. equal to the earth, 2. equal to gold, and so forth.
3. like the moon, 4. like fire, 5. like a great treasure,
6. equal to a mine of jewels, 7. equal to the great ocean, 8. equal to a diamond.
9. equal to a mountain, 10. equal to medicinal herbs, 11. equal to a spiritual friend.
12. Like a wish-fulfilling gem, 13. like the sun, 14. like a sweet song.
15. like a king, 16. like a storehouse, 17. like a great highway.
18. equal to a vehicle, 19. equal to spring water, 20. equal to an expression of joy.
21. like a river, 22. like a cloud;
and (gha) the limit.
The production of the thought of enlightenment by bodhisattvas is fourfold; namely:
that which pertains to the initial resolve on the stage of conduct through aspiration, and that which pertains to pure superior intention on the seven [bodhisattva] stages.
The fruition [wisdom] exists from the eighth stage onward,
while the unobstructed [wisdom] exists on the Buddha stage.
As it is said in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*:

The production of the thought of enlightenment is considered to be: that which consists of resolute conviction, another which consists of pure high resolve, that which is ripening on the stages, and likewise that which is free from obscurations.
2. Instruction (avavāda) consists of its characteristics,
divisions, and limits.
And the rule of hearing—thus the entire subject matter is set forth in two verses in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*. For it is said:

"Regarding practice, regarding the truths, regarding the three jewels beginning with the Buddha, regarding non-attachment, regarding lack of weariness, and regarding the complete grasping of the path."
The instruction is tenfold, to be understood with respect to the five eyes, the six qualities of superknowledge, the path of seeing, and that which is called the path of cultivation.

(a) The definition of the path to liberation is that instruction which is free from error; this constitutes its defining characteristic. Alternatively, the definition of Mahāyāna instruction is an unerring and pure teaching that consists of the means for attaining the sought-after goal by way of the arousal of the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) in the Mahāyāna.
(kha) There are two distinctions: first, instruction through training based on non-retrogression for the sake of ripening qualities already attained;
and subsequently, instruction through admonition based on the attainment of qualities not yet attained. Thus there are two distinctions.
Furthermore, instruction (avavāda) should be known as tenfold according to the distinction of its objects.
To explain: first is the instruction on practice (pratipatty-avavāda), which is training with respect to the mode of practice without transgressing the nature of the two truths.
As for the object of that practice, it consists of the four noble truths.
The instruction concerning that [truth] is the second, the instruction on the realization of truth (*satyāvavāda*).
That which is the basis—the three refuges—and the instruction concerning them is the third, the instruction on the Three Jewels (*ratnatrayāvavāda*).
That which is the cause for proceeding to excellence—non-attachment—and the teaching-instruction concerning it is the fourth.

The fifth is the instruction concerning the subject of indefatigability, which is the cause for not turning back. The sixth is the instruction concerning the subject of embracing the practice, which is the cause for not proceeding by another vehicle.
The seventh is the instruction concerning the five eyes, which is the cause for attaining independence from others.

The eighth is the instruction on the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), which has as its object the six superknowledges that are the cause for the complete fulfillment of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

The ninth is the instruction on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), which has as its object the path of seeing that completely eradicates in every way the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned by seeing, along with their seeds, which are of an imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*).

The tenth is the instruction on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), which has as its object the path of cultivation that completely eradicates in every way the innate obscurations (*sahajāvaraṇa*) to be abandoned by cultivation, along with their seeds.
(ga) The limit (*avadhi*): its boundary begins from the entry into the path and extends up to the stage of a Buddha (*buddhabhūmi*).
(gha) The rule of hearing (*śravaṇaniyama*).
Even one who has not yet entered the path—a person of pure resolute intention (*śuddhādhyāśayika*) and pure conduct (*śuddhakarmika*)—is capable of hearing the Mahāyāna instruction.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva who has entered the path hears instruction from many Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) over the course of many eons.
3. The Limbs of Penetration (*nirvedhāṅga*).

The characteristics, distinctions, limits, objects of focus, aspects, and so forth of the four types of aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), beginning with "heat" (*ūṣman*) and the rest, are set forth in two verses in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*. They are as follows:

"In terms of their object of focus, their aspect, their causality, and their thorough grasping, for those noble ones who partake in the respective conjunctions with the four conceptualizations," [the distinctions are explained].
The superiority of the Bodhisattva Protector over the Śrāvakas who possess the sword consists in his [attainments of] *uṣmagata* and the other stages, which are weak, medium, and intense.
(a) Definition:

The definition of the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) is that it is the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) arising immediately after the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and having its own cause.
This is the path of preparation.
The realization of the meaning (*arthābhisamaya*) and the factor of penetration (*nirvedhāṅga*) are not different in meaning. (kha) Distinction.
There are three paths of application (*prayogamārga*) for the three vehicles, beginning with that of the *śrāvaka*.
Within these three paths of application, there are four distinct divisions each—known as "heat" (*ūṣman*), "summit" (*mūrdhan*), "patience" (*kṣānti*), and "supreme mundane dharmas" (*agradharma*).
Thus, there are twelve divisions of the path of application.

The Mahāyāna path of preparation is the Mahāyāna clear realization of the object, arising from its own cause—the Mahāyāna path of equipment; it is the Mahāyāna path of preparation. The Mahāyāna path of preparation...
The realization of the meaning of the Mahāyāna and the aids to penetration of the Mahāyāna are synonyms;
they are the divisions of the path of preparation in the Mahāyāna.

The four aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), known as "heat," "summits," "patience," and "supreme mundane dharmas," are distinguished from the aids to penetration of the Śrāvakas by five specific excellences.
Each of these aids to penetration is further divided into three types—mild, medium, and intense.
Thus, twelve divisions of the path of application (*prayogamārga*) in the Mahāyāna arise.

(ga) Regarding the limit (*avadhi*): among the three kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*)— namely, the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*), the coarse selflessness of phenomena (*sthūla-dharma-nairātmya*), and the subtle selflessness of phenomena (*sūkṣma-dharma-nairātmya*)—

the application of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) extends from the attainment of insight (*vidarśanā*) that proceeds by taking any one of these selflessnesses as its object, up until the attainment of the [first] stage (*bhūmi*).
(g) The Mahāyāna path of preparation is distinguished from the Hīnayāna paths of preparation by six distinctions,
namely: by the distinction of the object (*ālambana-viśeṣa*), and so forth.
Due to the distinction of aspect,
the distinction of causality, and the distinction of thorough grasping.

This is due to the distinction in the association with the conceptualizations to be abandoned (*praheya-vikalpa-saṃyoga*) and the distinction in the differentiation of weak, medium, and intense degrees.
Furthermore, this excellence is clearly elucidated in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* by nine verses beginning with "The object is impermanence, etc. and ending with "the complete grasping in every way."
This has been explained.
4. The basis of practice: the natural lineage (*prakṛtiguṇa*) is the basis for the practice of the Mahāyāna.
Its characteristics and so forth are described in two verses in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*. For instance:
Of the dharma of sixfold realization, of the abandonment of the opposites,
of the employment of those two, and of wisdom together with compassion.
The lineage (gotra) is said to be the foundation for the non-commonality with disciples, for the sequence of activity for the sake of others, and for the effortless operation of gnosis.
(a) Regarding the definition:
that which is the *dharmadhātu*, when purified, transforms into awakening— that is the definition of the lineage (*gotra*).

Specifically, that which, when the dharmadhātu has been purified, is transformed into unexcelled perfect enlightenment and serves as the basis for the practice of the Mahāyāna, is called the natural lineage (*prakṛtiguṇa*).
(kha) As for the classification, from the perspective of terminology, there are two types: the innate lineage (*prakṛtigotra*) and the cultivated lineage (*paripuṣṭagotra*).
The innate lineage, which serves as the basis for the practice of the Mahāyāna, becomes thirteenfold when viewed from the perspective of the dharmas that depend upon it.
This very natural lineage (*prakṛtigoratra*) also serves as the basis for the Mahāyāna path of equipment (*sambhāramārga*).
It consists of four bases for the four types of mundane aids to penetration (*laukikanirvedhabhāgīya*) known as "heat," "summits," "patience," and "supreme mundane dharmas";
and it is one basis for the supramundane path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
There is one basis for the supramundane path of cultivation; thus, there are six natural lineages (*prakṛtigoratra*).
Following that, there is the basis for the practice of the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*), and following that, the basis for the practice of abandonment (*prahāṇa*).

Immediately following that, it is the support for the path of liberation, which consists in the departure from conceptual constructions associated with the arising and ceasing of those [afflictions] through the non-perception of anything to be abandoned by their respective antidotes;
thereafter, it is the support for wisdom and compassion,
and the support for the qualities uncommon to the Śrāvakas and others.

The basis for the sequence of benefiting others and the basis for the effortless operation of gnosis— these are the thirteen divisions of the lineage abiding in the fundamental nature (*prakṛtisthagotra*). (ga) The Limit.
Its limit begins from the path of the equipment (*sambhāra-mārga*) of the Mahāyāna and extends up to the stage of the Bodhisattva abiding in the final moment.

Furthermore, it should be understood that its pervasiveness specifically begins from the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) on the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) explicitly taught above, and extends up to the stage of the Bodhisattva abiding in the final moment.
5. The objective support (*ālambana*) of the practice.
In this context, three things are explained: the characteristic, the classification, and the limit of the objects of practice.
In the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, the essential nature of the object is demonstrated by two verses; for it is said:
"The object consists of all phenomena, which are further [categorized as] wholesome and so forth."
Those known as mundane attainments and those considered supramundane;

those phenomena that are with outflows and those without outflows; those that are conditioned and those that are unconditioned; and those qualities shared with the disciples and those unique to the Sage.
(a) Definition: The definition of the object of comprehension (*ālambana*) is that its very nature as an object of cognition constitutes its status as an objective support.
(b) Classification.
The object of focus is of eleven kinds; namely:
the three types of bodily action and so forth—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—and the five aggregates associated with ordinary worldlings.
The four untainted meditative absorptions (*anāsrava-dhyāna*) embraced by all noble beings;
the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*), because they are not the antidote to the view of self;
and the four untainted applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), because they are the antidote to the view of self.

Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*)— such as the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika*) and so forth— are comprised within the realms of desire and the rest, being dependent upon causes and conditions (the Truth of the Path).
Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*)— such as suchness (*tathatā*) and so forth— are not included within the three realms and are independent of causes (the Truth of Cessation).
The qualities such as the four dhyānas that arise from the mental continuums of all noble beings,
and the ten powers— the dharmas arising from the continuum of a perfectly enlightened Buddha— which are uncommon [to others], constitute the elevenfold object of focus.
(ga) The limit.

It should be understood that because all phenomena are apprehended exactly as they are according to the sequence of realization, there is no limit to the stages (*bhūmi*) of the objects of focus (*ālambana*).
6. Summary of Practice (*pratipatti-samuddeśa*):
Its three aspects—characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), classification (*bheda*), and limit (*avadhi*)—are to be fully known.
These are indicated by this single verse in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*:
"The objective of the Noble Self-Existent Ones is to be understood through three greatnesses regarding the three— supremacy over all beings, the mind, and the triad of abandonment and realization."
(a) Regarding the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*):
for a bodhisattva established in practice, the very object of his own practice is the "designation of practice" (*pratipatti-samuddeśa*); this is the characteristic.
(b) The classification (*bheda*).
Its three divisions are: the greatness of the mind consisting in being supreme among all sentient beings, the greatness of abandonment, and the greatness of realization.
(ga) The limit: this summary is fulfilled only on the stage of a Buddha.
7. The practice of armor.
Its definition and other characteristics are described in this way by a single verse in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*:
"The practice of armor, which consists of the summary of each of those sixfold [perfections] such as giving and so forth, is explained as being sixfold by means of six sets of six."

The characteristic of practice is the activity which, based on the generation of the mind of the Great Vehicle, serves for the accomplishment of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; it consists generally, within the domain of the three types of omniscience, in the foundation of pure dharmas, and specifically,
in each of the fourfold clear realizations beginning with the complete awakening to all aspects, in the foundation of the six perfections.
This is the characteristic of the practice of the Mahāyāna. Regarding the divisions of practice,
this Mahāyāna practice is fourfold.
Namely: the practice of armor,
the practice of setting out,
and the practice of equipment.
And the practice of departure (*niryāṇapratipatti*).
(a) The characteristic of the practice of armor (*sannāhapratipatti*):

the application of sentient beings (*sattvayoga*) undertaken by means of the wisdom that subsumes each of the six perfections within the six perfections is the characteristic of the practice of armor.
The practice of armor (*sannāhapratipatti*) and the path of the bodhisattva (*bodhisattvamārga*) are not different in meaning.

(b) As for its divisions: starting from the practice of the armor of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) up to the practice of the armor of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), there are six divisions.
In the case of giving as well, there are the six perfections, beginning with giving and morality;
thus, by taking each of the six perfections as having its own set of six, there are thirty-six divisions in detail. (ga) The limit.
Its limit extends from the bodhisattva on the path of equipment (*sambhāramārga*) up to the bodhisattva abiding in the final moment.
8. The practice of setting out (*prasthānapratipatti*):
its essential nature is described by two verses in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*. For it is said:
In the meditations and formless attainments, in giving and the rest, in the path, in loving-kindness and the like,
in the application of the perception of objects, and in the purifications of the three spheres.
In the summary, in the six superknowledges, and in the method of the knowledge of all aspects,
the practice of setting out is to be known as that which mounts the Great Vehicle.
(a) Definition:

The definition of the practice of setting out (*prasthāna-pratipatti*) is the act of setting out toward the Dharma—which consists of either the cause or the fruit—within the Mahāyāna, by means of a practice characterized primarily by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). (b) Classification: [The classification is as follows:]...
This practice of setting forth should be known as ninefold;
for instance, there is the setting forth in the meditative absorptions and formless attainments,
and the setting forth in the six perfections beginning with generosity.
Setting out upon the noble paths, setting out upon the four immeasurables, and setting out upon the yoga of non-apprehension.
Setting out in the purities of the three spheres;
setting out in the three types of objectives, beginning with being supreme among all sentient beings;
and setting out in the six supernormal knowledges.
Regarding "the setting out toward the knowledge of all aspects" (*sarvākārajñatā*):

its limit is defined as beginning from the stage of heat (*uṣmagata*) on the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) belonging to the level of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*), and extending up to the Bodhisattva abiding in the final moment. This constitutes its boundary.

9. The Practice of Accumulation: All the characteristics and other aspects of this practice have been correctly elucidated in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* by means of two verses. As it is said: "Compassion, the sixfold set beginning with giving, calm abiding together with insight,"
And that which is the path of union, and that which is skillfulness in means.
Knowledge, merit, the path, the dhāraṇīs, and the ten stages— these, along with the counteractive measures, should be understood as the sequence of the practice of the accumulations.
(a) Its definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is: practice consisting of the accumulations (*sambhāra-pratipatti*) which directly bestows great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), the fruit that is the self.
(b) Its classification (*bheda*).
There are seventeen divisions of this practice of the accumulations, namely:
the accumulation of great compassion, the accumulation of generosity, and so forth.
The equipment of ethical discipline, the equipment of patience, and the equipment of vigor.
The equipment of meditative concentration, the equipment of wisdom,
and the equipment of calm abiding.
the equipment of clear vision,
the equipment of the union of the two,
and the equipment of skill in means;
The accumulation of knowledge, the accumulation of merit,
and the accumulation of the path.
The equipment of dhāraṇīs, the equipment of the stages,
and the equipment of the remedies.
(ga) As for the limit: although it exists even on the stage of the beginner as a mere accumulation,

those accumulations which are explicitly taught as leading to the attainment of great enlightenment begin from the state of the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) belonging to the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) and continue until the state of the bodhisattva abiding in the final moment.

There are fifteen preparations for the equipment (sambhāra-pratipatti) from the beginning up to the stage of the supreme mundane dharmas (agradharma) belonging to the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga).
The sixteenth is the equipment for the stages (bhūmi-sambhāra), and the seventeenth is the equipment for the antidotes (pratipakṣa-sambhāra); these two exist throughout the ten stages.
10. The practice of departure (*niryāṇapratipatti*).
Its essential nature is correctly demonstrated in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* by two verses. For it is said:
"In the summary, in equanimity, in the welfare of beings, and in the absence of effort..."
And there is the departure for the ultimate, which is characterized by attainment;
and there is the departure into the knowledge of all aspects, which has the path as its domain.
This eightfold nature is to be known as the practice of departure.
(a) The definition:

The practice of departure (*niryāṇapratipatti*) is defined as the application of beings belonging to the pure stages (*śuddhabhūmika*), which leads exclusively to the state of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
(b) The classification.
This practice of departure consists of eight aspects,
namely: departure through the threefold objective, and departure in equality.
Departure for the sake of sentient beings, effortless departure,
and ultimate departure.
The departure through attainment, the departure through the knowledge of all aspects, and the departure through the path.
(ga) Limit: Its pervasion occurs only within the three pure stages (*śuddhabhūmi*).
Thus end the ten factors that characterize the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
(ā) Eleven factors characterizing the knowledge of the paths:
1. the limbs of the knowledge of the paths, beginning with the act of eclipsing;
2. the path of the śrāvakas.
3. the path of the solitary buddha (pratyekabuddhamārga), 4. the path of the bodhisattva (bodhisattvamārga), 5. the activity of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārgakāritra).
6. Adhimukti regarding the path of cultivation; 7. Praise, laudation, and eulogy of one who possesses adhimukti regarding the path of cultivation; 8. Dedication.

9. Rejoicing (*anumodanā*), 10. Accomplishment (*abhinirhāraḥ*), and 11. Ultimate Purity (*atyantaviśuddhiḥ*): these eleven factors characterize the Knowledge of the Path (*mārgajñatā*). The stages of darkening and so forth, as well as the paths of the disciples and the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddhas],
constitute the path of seeing with great benefits through its qualities pertaining to this life and the next.
Activity, resolute belief, and being praised, extolled, and lauded;
as well as the two unsurpassed mental attentions regarding dedication and sympathetic joy.
Accomplishment and ultimate purity—this is the path of cultivation for wise Bodhisattvas; thus is the knowledge of the paths proclaimed.

1. Regarding the "obscuration" (*dhyāmīkaraṇatā*) and so forth—the characteristics and all other aspects of the factors conducive to the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñatā*) beginning with obscuration—all are described by a single verse in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*. For it says:
"The obscuration [of the gods] by [the Bodhisattva's] radiance is for the sake of their fitness."
The object, the restriction, the pervasion, its intrinsic nature, and its activity.
(ka) The definition (*lakṣaṇa*):
The qualities (*guṇa*) that fulfill the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñatā*), having become constituent parts, are themselves the limbs of the knowledge of the path; this is the definition.

Alternatively—the definition is that the qualities residing within the mental continuum of sentient beings, which fulfill the knowledge of the path and are explicitly indicated in this context, are the limbs of the knowledge of the path.

(kha) The distinction consists of the five limbs of the knowledge of the paths, beginning with the act of darkening [the light of the gods], as follows: the basis, which is the absence of immediate ego-grasping;
The co-operative condition is the arising of the thought of enlightenment;
pervasion together with its cause is its nature; and not abandoning cyclic existence is its essential character.
Regarding "the embracing of sentient beings who have not been embraced": (ga) as for the limit,
generally taking the non-entry into the path as the starting point, the boundary extends up to the stage of a Buddha.
With respect to the path of accumulation (*sambhāramārga*), the limit for those factors explicitly taught extends from that point up to the stage of the Bodhisattva abiding in the final moment.
2. The Śrāvaka Path:
The characteristics and other aspects of the realization of the Śrāvaka path are correctly demonstrated by a single verse written below in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*. To wit:
Through the non-apprehension of the aspects of the four noble truths,
this path of the Śrāvakas is to be known within the system of the Knowledge of Paths.
(a) Regarding its definition:

for the sake of favoring those disciples who belong to the lineage of the Śrāvakas, the realization of a Mahāyāna noble one that is established by way of directly perceiving any one of the sixteen aspects—such as impermanence and so forth—by taking any one of the four noble truths, such as suffering and so forth, as its object; being of the same type as the realization of a Śrāvaka, it is called the "knowledge of the path" (*mārgajñatā*) that knows the Śrāvaka path.
(kha) As for its divisions: by way of the view of aspects, it is sixteenfold;
but by way of the path, it is threefold, through the distinction between the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning.

(ga) Its limit extends from the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) up to the stage of a Buddha (*buddhabhūmi*). According to the opinion of some, its limit begins from the path of accumulation for the Mahāyāna (*mahāyānasambhāramārga*) up to the stage of a Buddha.
3. The Path of the Pratyekabuddha:

All aspects of the realization of a pratyekabuddha, such as its characteristics and so forth, are set forth in three verses in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*. For it is said: "The self-arisen ones [attain] self-awakening because instruction by others is useless."
And the profundity of their knowledge is said to belong to the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddhas].
For whatever purpose, wherever, and in whatever manner one serves another, that very purpose— though even devoid of fame— becomes renowned in that same place and in that same manner.

The summary of the rhinoceros-like path should be understood through the abandonment of the conceptualization of the apprehended object, the non-abandonment of the apprehending subject, and its basis.
(a) The definition:

For the sake of favoring those disciples belonging to the lineage of the pratyekabuddhas, the Mahāyānist clear realization of the same type as the attainment of a pratyekabuddha— which is established through the vision of knowledge that directly realizes the emptiness of external objects of apprehension by taking the twelve sense bases as its object— is the "knowledge of the path" regarding the path of the pratyekabuddhas.
(kha) The distinction consists of the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
Regarding the "path of no-more-learning" (*aśaikṣamārga*), there are three divisions of it:
(ga) its limit (*avadhi*): the boundary of this path extends from the beginning of the Mahāyāna path of seeing up to the stage of a Buddha (*buddhabhūmi*).
4. The Mahāyāna Path of Seeing:
the characteristics and divisions of the path of seeing which possesses great benefits.
The limit (*avadhi*)—these three are to be fully understood; here they are briefly described.
In the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, their essential nature is demonstrated by five verses.
(a) The definition (*lakṣaṇa*).

The definition is that the realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), characterized by the cessation of the two extremes of existence and peace, is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the Mahāyāna.
(kha) As for its divisions, there are two divisions of the path of seeing: meditative equipoise knowledge (*samāhitajñāna*) and subsequently attained knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdhajñāna*).
Through the vision of knowledge, there are three knowledges that constitute the path of seeing:
the first is that which knows the path of the śrāvaka, which is itself the path of seeing; the second is that which knows the path of the pratyekabuddha.
The third [category] is that which knows the Mahāyāna path; thus there are three divisions.

Through the perspective of the object (*ālambana*) and the perspective of the turning away (*vyāvṛtti*), sixteen divisions are to be understood: namely, eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and eight cognitions (*jñāna*).
(ga) Its limit is that its pervasion occurs only on the first bodhisattva stage;
this is the activity of the path of cultivation.
The characteristics and other attributes of the functions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) are clearly demonstrated in a single verse of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*. For it says:
"Subduing in every respect means the complete conquest of the afflictions;
it is the state of being invulnerable to assault, awakening, and the venerability of the support."
(a) Definition:
The definition of the activity of the path of cultivation is the attainment of benefits through the power of cultivating the realization of reality.
(b) Classification: [The classification is as follows:]
This has six divisions, namely: the practice of self-restraint through the negation of self-exaltation,
and the practice of bowing to all beings.
The activity of overcoming the afflictions such as attachment; the activity of being invulnerable to assaults resulting from the infliction of harm by others;
and the activity of practicing for the sake of perfect awakening.
The function consists in being the support for the perfection of wisdom, its object, and that which is worthy of worship.
(ga) Its limit extends from the first stage up to the tenth stage; this constitutes its boundary.
The path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is discussed here under three headings: its definition (*lakṣaṇa*), its divisions (*bheda*), and its limits (*avadhi*).
(a) The definition:
The Mahāyāna subsequent realization is the Mahāyāna path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); this is its defining characteristic.
"Subsequent realization" and "path of cultivation" are synonymous terms. (b) Classification.
There are two divisions: the contaminated path of cultivation and the uncontaminated path of cultivation.
Among these, the contaminated is the conceptual path of cultivation, while the uncontaminated is the non-conceptual.
In that regard, the mundane (*sāsrava*) [mental engagement] characterized by resolute belief (*adhimukti*), dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), and rejoicing (*anumodanā*) is threefold.
The supramundane (*anāsrava*), however, is twofold: accomplishment (*abhinirhāra*) and the nature of ultimate purity (*atyantaviśuddhi-svabhāva*).
This is the resolute belief of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga-adhimukti*).

The entire characteristics and so forth of the path of cultivation consisting of resolute belief (*adhimukti-bhāvanāmārga*) have been clearly demonstrated in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* by means of two verses. For it is said:

"Resolute belief should be known as threefold: that which has its own benefit, that which has the benefit of both self and others, and that which has the benefit of others alone; and each of these is further held to be threefold."
It is weak, medium, and intense; and that [weak one] is further divided into weak-weak and so forth.
Thus, being threefold in this way, it is considered to be twenty-seven types.
(a) The definition:

The path of cultivation known as "resolute belief" (*adhimukti*)—which is the Mahāyānist subsequent realization established by means of firm conviction regarding the Mother of the Victors (*jinajananī*), who is the source for one's own benefit, the benefit of others, and the benefit of all—is characterized as being conceptual (*savikalpa*). This is the definition.

(kha) As for its divisions: by way of its fundamental classification, resolution (*adhimukti*) is threefold—namely, that which is for one’s own benefit, that which is for the benefit of both oneself and others, and that which is for the benefit of others alone.
Even while being threefold, because each is further divided according to the distinctions of weak, medium, and intense, it becomes ninefold through three sets of three.
For example, there is weak, medium, and intense conviction regarding one's own welfare;
likewise, there is conviction regarding the welfare of both oneself and others, and conviction regarding the welfare of others.

Thus, this ninefold conviction, when each is further divided according to the distinctions of the nine types beginning with "weak-weak," becomes twenty-seven types through the multiplication of three by nine.
Namely: the weak-weak, the weak-medium, and the weak-strong.
medium-weak, medium-medium, and medium-strong;
The weak-in-the-strong, the medium-in-the-strong,
and the strong-in-the-strong— these are the nine types of resolute belief directed toward one's own welfare.
Likewise, they should be understood in terms of the conviction regarding one's own and others' welfare, and the conviction regarding others' welfare.
(ga) Regarding the limit: starting from the first stage up to the tenth stage constitutes its boundary.
Some maintain that this begins from the second bhūmi and extends up to the tenth bhūmi.

7. Praise, laudation, and eulogy for one who has attained conviction through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*): the characteristics and other aspects of the praise and so forth for a bodhisattva who has attained conviction through the path of cultivation are described by a single verse in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*. To that effect:
Praise, exultation, and commendation regarding the perfection of wisdom are held to consist of three sets of nine stages of resolute conviction.
(a) The definition (*lakṣaṇa*):

For the purpose of increasing the enthusiasm of the bodhisattva who practices the previously mentioned threefold faith and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the praise and so forth performed toward that faith are characterized by the realization of the object as it truly is; they are not of the nature of mere empty rhetoric—this is the definition.
(kha) The classification is as before, consisting of exactly twenty-seven subdivisions. (ga) The limit.
It is like the path of cultivation consisting of resolute belief (*adhimukti-bhāvanāmārga*).
8. The dedication of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga-pariṇāmanā*):
all aspects of this dedication, such as its characteristics and divisions, are clearly demonstrated in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* by three verses. For instance:
The excellence, however, is its transformation; that is its supreme activity. It is characterized by non-apprehension and has non-perversion as its defining mark.
It is secluded, the sphere of mindfulness whose nature is the flood of the Buddha's merit;
it possesses skillful means, is signless, and is approved by the Buddhas.
Furthermore, there is another threefold dedication that does not enter into the three realms;
it consists of the mild, the medium, and the intense, and its nature is the arising of great merit.
(kā) The definition:

The Mahāyāna path of cultivation called "dedication" is defined as that conceptual realization of a Mahāyānist which dedicates one's own and others' bases of meritorious action consisting of wholesome deeds toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment. This is its definition.
(kha) This differentiation of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is twelvefold, namely: the mental attention of superior transformation (*viśeṣapariṇāmanāmanaskāra*).
the mental attention of dedication characterized by non-apprehension, the mental attention of dedication characterized by non-perversion,
and the mental attention of secluded dedication.
the mental attention of dedication through the recollection of the nature of the flood of the Buddha’s merit;
the mental attention of dedication through skill in means; and the mental attention of signless dedication.
the mental application of dedication authorized (or approved) by the Buddhas,
and the mental application of dedication that is not included within the three realms;

There are twelve divisions: the mental application of weak dedication consisting of the arising of great merit, the mental application of middling dedication consisting of the arising of great merit, and the mental application of superior dedication consisting of the arising of great merit.
(ga) Limit: Beginning from the first stage, the Joyous (*pramuditā*), up to the tenth stage, this constitutes the boundary of this mental application of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-manaskāra*).
9. Rejoicing belonging to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

The characteristics, distinctions, and other aspects of the mental attention of rejoicing (*anumodanā-manaskāra*) are described in this way by means of a single verse in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*: "Herein, the cultivation of the mental attention of rejoicing is prescribed as follows: one rejoices in the roots of virtue through both skillful means and non-apprehension."
(a) Definition:

The definition is that the Mahāyāna path of cultivation consisting of rejoicing—which is a conceptual realization—whereby one rejoices in the bases of meritorious action consisting of the wholesome deeds of oneself and others, is called the Mahāyāna path of cultivation known as "rejoicing. This is its definition.

(kha) As for the classification of the mental attention of rejoicing (*anumodanā-manaskāra*), there are two types of classification: namely, rejoicing in one's own bases of meritorious action (*kuśala-puṇya-kriyā-vastu*), and...
Rejoicing in the bases of meritorious action consisting of the wholesome deeds of others;
or alternatively, the mental application of rejoicing that has the conventional as its object and the mental application of rejoicing that has the ultimate as its object. (ga) The limit.
The limits of the three mental orientations—of resolute belief, dedication, and sympathetic joy—are identical across all stages.
10. Accomplishment:
The characteristics and other features of the path of cultivation that accomplishes the untainted are set forth in a single verse in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*. For it says:
Its excellence of intrinsic nature is the non-conditioning of all things;
its great purpose is the dedication of phenomena through non-apprehension.
(a) The definition:
the Mahāyāna realization free from outflows,
which establishes the function of ultimate comprehension.
Its characteristic is that it is the Mahāyāna path of cultivation known as "actualization" (*abhinirhāra*).
(b) As for its divisions, there are five types of divisions.
That is to say: the nature [of the path] is the non-erroneous vision of all phenomena, such as form and so forth;

the excellence of the path of cultivation consists in the fact that the attainment of Buddhahood occurs in no other way; and the application toward realization is without volitional effort, by virtue of not producing any distinction among all phenomena.
It is an "offering" because all phenomena are non-apprehendable from the perspective of ultimate reality;
it is "of great purpose" because it accomplishes the great purpose that is Buddhahood. (ga) The limit.
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the tenth stage, this constitutes the limit of its accomplishment.
11. Absolute Purity:

All characteristics and so forth of the uncontaminated path of cultivation (*anāsrava-bhāvanāmārga*), which is termed "absolute purity," have been very clearly elucidated by means of three verses in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*. For instance:
The purity of the fruit is indeed the purity of form and so forth; since there is no difference or separation between these two, it is thus called "purity."

Purification is absolute for the Buddha at all times, due to his abandonment of the three paths of afflictions and the knowable by those who are disciples, rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddhas], and the sons of the Victor.
The path beginning with the weakest-of-the-weak serves as purification across the nine stages,
acting as the antidote to the stains beginning with the strongest-of-the-strong.
(a) The definition:
the Mahāyāna uncontaminated clear realization,
which establishes the function of the final abandonment.

Its characteristic is that it is called the "path of cultivation of ultimate purity" (*atyantaviśuddhi*) within the Mahāyāna. (b) As for its divisions: there are nine paths of cultivation, beginning with the "mild-mild" (*mṛdu-mṛdu*), which serve as the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) to the nine opposing factors (*vipakṣa*) to be abandoned by the path of cultivation; these constitute the divisions of this path of cultivation of ultimate purity.
(ga) The limit (*avadhi*) is from the first stage up to the tenth stage; this constitutes the boundary of this path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Thus are the eleven factors that characterize the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*).
(i) Nine factors characterizing omniscience:
1. By means of wisdom, not abiding in existence; 2. By means of compassion, not remaining in quiescence.
3. remoteness from the Mother of the Victors due to lack of skillful means; 4. non-remoteness due to skillful means; 5. the adverse factors.
6. Antidote, 7. Application, 8.
Equanimity.

9. The path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and [the other stages]—these nine factors characterize omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). This has been correctly stated in two verses of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*: "By means of wisdom (*prajñā*), one does not abide in existence (*bhava*); by means of compassion (*karuṇā*), one does not abide in peace (*śama*).
Through lack of skillful means (*anupāya*), there is remoteness; through skillful means (*upāya*), there is no remoteness."
The path of seeing for the Śrāvakas and others is held to consist of the discordant factors and their antidotes, the application, and its equality; this is omniscience.
1. Through wisdom (*prajñā*), there is no abiding in existence; 2. through compassion (*karuṇā*), there is no dwelling in [personal] peace.
The characteristics and so forth of both are set forth in a single verse in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*. For it is said:
Neither on this shore nor on the further shore, nor situated in between the two,
the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is considered such because of the knowledge of the equality of the paths.
In this regard, the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and other attributes of both are explained here individually.
Not abiding in existence by means of wisdom is its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

The characteristic of this omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is the wisdom belonging to the lineage of the Mahāyāna, which dwells within the mental continuum of a Mahāyānist, possesses the essence of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and directly realizes the sixteen aspects beginning with impermanence (*anitya*).

Furthermore, this perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) of the Bodhisattvas does not abide in the extreme of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) because, through wisdom, they perceive the defects of cyclic existence.
(b) The Distinction.
There are three divisions: the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).

The Mahāyāna path of cultivation, which directly realizes the sixteen aspects—such as impermanence and so forth—connected with the four noble truths beginning with suffering, is the indicator of this omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), whose characteristic nature is that "there is no place for wisdom to abide."
The characteristic [of this omniscience] is not abiding in peace out of compassion; rather,
the Mahāyāna realization— which, through great compassion, turns back from the extreme of peace that relies on conventional reality— is the characteristic of this omniscience.
And this perfection of wisdom, because it accomplishes the welfare of sentient beings through compassion, does not abide in the extreme of the peace of *nirvāṇa*.

The great compassion residing in the mental continuum of noble persons on the Mahāyāna path of cultivation—by means of this compassion, there is no abiding in quiescence—is the defining characteristic of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*). (b) The classification.
For a noble follower of the Mahāyāna, there are three types of great compassion— those having sentient beings as their object, those having phenomena as their object, and those being objectless—
and there are also distinctions such as the arousal of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).

Because of the realization of the equality of all phenomena belonging to the three times through the aspect of their non-arising, there is the Perfection of Wisdom of the Bodhisattvas, which is remote from the sphere of the Śrāvakas and others.
Furthermore, it is not established on the near shore of saṃsāra, nor on the far shore of nirvāṇa;
nor is it established even in between, in the middle, because there is no real entity existing between both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Through the correct penetration of wisdom and compassion, one is free from the apprehension of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
(ga) The limit extends from the first stage, the Joyous (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), up to the Buddha-stage; this constitutes the boundary of both.
3. Its remoteness due to lack of skillful means (*anupāya*)—all its characteristics and so forth—are clearly set forth by half a verse in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*. For it says:
"It is remote through lack of skillful means, because of the apprehension of signs."

(a) The definition [of the Śrāvakas and others] is as follows: because they lack the knowledge of the equality of the three times, their knowledge—which directly realizes the aspects such as impermanence—is distant from the Mother of the Victors due to the conjunction with perception of signs and the deficiency of compassion and wisdom;
this is the definition.

(kha) As for the distinction (*bheda*): there is a twofold distinction, namely, the knowledge of the aspects such as impermanence residing in the continuum of a *śrāvaka*, and the knowledge of the aspects such as impermanence residing in the continuum of a *pratyekabuddha*. (ga) As for the limit (*avadhi*): [the text continues].
Its limit extends from the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) up to the stage of arhatship.
4. Its proximity through skillful means (*upāya*) in the presentation of its characteristics and so forth has been correctly accomplished by half a verse in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*. For it is said:
Through skill in means, its correct proximity has been declared.

(ka) Its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is the knowledge of the aspects of impermanence and so forth, which—though belonging to those of the Hīnayāna lineage—is acquired by Mahāyāna practitioners through great compassion and the wisdom that directly realizes emptiness.

However, for Bodhisattvas and others who have eliminated the delusive signs of the adherence to the notion of intrinsic existence, the thorough knowledge of all phenomena such as form is itself the thorough knowledge of their equality; therefore, there is a state of being correctly near to the Mother [Prajñāpāramitā].
(kha) The distinction is that it is the Mahāyāna path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
There are three divisions: the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*). (ga) The limit.
The boundary begins from the Mahāyāna path of seeing and extends up to the stage of a Buddha (buddhabhūmi).
5. Regarding its adverse factors (vipakṣa) and other characteristics, they have been very clearly explained in a single verse in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*. For instance:
Regarding the emptiness of the aggregates such as form, regarding phenomena belonging to the three times,
and regarding the factors conducive to enlightenment such as generosity— the notion that there is "practice" therein constitutes an adverse factor.
(ka) The definition:

The knowledge of things (*vastujñatā*) belonging to the Hīnayāna is characterized by being dissociated from both great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatāprajñā*); its intrinsic nature consists in the apprehension of entities.

It is defined as such because it perceives all things—form and so forth, as well as all phenomena of the three times, whether they pertain to the contaminated, the uncontaminated, or both—as being non-apprehensible in their essential nature, yet everywhere apprehends them as entities, [thereby realizing] their emptiness of the self and so forth imagined by others.

[These] have been seen. However, the notion of practice (*anuṣṭhāna-saṃjñā*), although it serves as their antidote, becomes an adverse factor (*vipakṣa*) because it must be abandoned due to its being an active misconception (*viparyāsa*). (kha) The classification; (ga) the limit.
Just as its differentiation and limit were both demonstrated in the manner of the section beginning with "distance through lack of means," so too [is it] "from the object of knowledge" (jñeyāt).
6. The counter-position (pratipakṣaḥ).

All its characteristics, distinctions, and so forth have been demonstrated in detail through three verses in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*. For it is said: "The absence of egoism regarding giving and the other perfections, the enjoining of others to them, and the negation of attachment to even the Buddhas and so forth—this is subtle attachment."
That profundity arises from the very nature of discernment regarding the path of phenomena;
it is a knowledge of a single essence, which is the relinquishing of attachment to all phenomena.
Its difficulty to comprehend is declared by the negation of [seeing] and so forth;
its inconceivability is maintained because it is not cognized through form and the other [sensory objects].

(a) Its definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is the knowledge of things (*vastujñatā*) abiding in the mental continuum of a Mahāyāna noble one, which is embraced by both great compassion and the wisdom that directly realizes emptiness, and whose nature consists of the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*).
(b) Its classification (*bheda*) and its limit (*avadhi*).
Both should be understood exactly as they were described previously in the context of "proximity through means. The distinction lies in that,
for the Mother of the Victors (*jinajananī*), there is both distance and non-distance from the knowledge of things (*vastujñatā*, i.e., omniscience).
There are two divisions:
the proximity to the Mother of the Victors who has become the fruit, preceded by the Hīnayāna;
and proximity through skillful means.
The four synonyms are: the counteragent, the knowledge of things belonging to the Mahāyāna, and so forth;
these constitute the remoteness from the Mother of the Victors who has become the fruit.
Remoteness due to lack of skillful means,
being bound by the apprehension of signs and grasping,
and the presence of opposing factors.
And "knowledge of the objects of the Hīnayāna" are synonyms.
This distinction between the adverse factors and their antidotes for the Śrāvakas, Bodhisattvas, and others should be understood exactly as it has been explained.
And so it has been said:

Having established it in this way, one should understand that this entire classification of the discordant factors and their remedies is presented within the system of omniscience as previously described.
Moreover:

"For śrāvakas and others, such practice constitutes a distancing from their mother; although it is an antidote for them, because it proceeds from the misconception of apprehending real entities, it is to be abandoned by bodhisattvas and is thus a discordant factor (*vipakṣa*).
7. Application (*prayoga*).

All its characteristics, distinctions, and so forth have been explained in detail in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* by means of two and a half verses of the *kārikā* text. For it says: "In form and so forth, in their impermanence and so forth, in their non-filling and filling, and in the non-attachment to them—therein lies the practice of conduct through negation."
It is unchanging and not an agent, yet its threefold application is difficult to perform;
it is unfailing and esteemed because it brings about the attainment of fruit according to one's capacity.
And that which is independent of others and which makes known the sevenfold [nature]—this is the definition.

Regarding the conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), the essential nature of things and their specific qualities, the "application" (*prayoga*) is a spiritual practice belonging to the lineage of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) that serves as the antidote to the adherence to perception which proceeds from cognitive error (*viparyāsa*). This is its definition.
(kha) The classification of the application is tenfold,
as follows: the negation of adherence to the reality of form and so forth;
The negation of adherence to them as real with respect to their specific qualities such as impermanence and so forth;
the non-fulfillment with respect to imagined forms; and the fulfillment with respect to the forms of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
In the perfections, there is, from the perspective of ultimate reality, neither decrease nor increase (i.e., immutability),

and from the perspective of ultimate reality, the absence of an agent; furthermore, there is the difficulty of [the three types of omniscience]— consisting of the summary, the application, and the performance— respectively.

There are ten divisions: non-futility through the attainment of the fruit according to one's capacity; independence from others regarding the awakening of great benefit; and the knowledge of the sevenfold manifestation, such as transformation and so forth, which is like a dream.
(ga) Its limit (avadhi) extends from the path of accumulation (sambhāramārga) up to the state of the Bodhisattva abiding in the final moment; this is its boundary.
8. Equality (samatā).
Its essential nature is shown by half a verse in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*. For it says:
"Non-conceptualization regarding that [object] in terms of form and so forth is considered its fourfold equality.
This is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*).

The characteristic of equality (*samatā*) consists in the non-conceptualization (*amananā*) of the knowing subject and the known phenomena associated with the modes of application regarding the tenfold objects mentioned above.
(b) As for its divisions: since there are four instances of non-conceptualization for each of the ten previously mentioned modes of application, there are forty subdivisions of this equality.

And it is said in the *Āloka-ṭīkā*: “Thus, by the negation of the mental engagement with categories such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth; the mental engagement with signs (*nimitta*) such as blue and so forth; the mental engagement with the manifold elaborations (*prapañca*) such as ‘form is twofold, twentyfold,’ and so on; and the mental engagement with the realization of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and so forth—the non-perception of the dharmas of the knower and the known is stated to be fourfold; this is how it should be understood.”
(ga) The limit (*avadhi*) of this equality extends from the path of accumulation (*sambhāramārga*) up to the state of the Bodhisattva abiding in the final moment.
9. The Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
All its characteristics and so forth have been set forth in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* by means of five verses.
(a) Regarding the characteristic:
the characteristic is that the path of seeing is the realization of the truths, which is empty of the thirty-two superimpositions.
(kha) Regarding the distinctions: due to the differentiation of the three vehicles and the three paths of vision, these sixteen moments themselves constitute its sixteen distinctions.
Thus, there are nine factors that characterize omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
2. The thirty-six factors characterizing the four applications:
therein, there are eleven factors characterizing the realization of all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*), and eight factors characterizing the peak realization (*mūrdhābhisamaya*).
There are thirty-six factors: thirteen factors that characterize the gradual realization (*ānupūrvikābhisamaya*), four that characterize the realization in a single moment (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodha*),
and eleven factors that characterize the realization of all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*).
1. aspects, 2. applications, 3. qualities, 4. faults.
5. The characteristics, 6. the factors conducive to liberation, 7. the factors conducive to penetration.
8. the irreversible assembly; 9. the equality of existence and peace;
10. the unsurpassed purity of the field.

11. The eleven factors known as skill in means (*upāyakauśala*) characterize the realization of all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*); this is demonstrated by two verses in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*. For it is said:

The aspects (*ākāra*), along with their applications (*prayoga*), virtues (*guṇa*), and faults (*doṣa*) together with their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); the aids to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*); the learner (*śaikṣa*), and the group of those who are irreversible (*avaivartika*).
The equality of existence and peace, the supreme purification of the field,
and the complete awakening in all its aspects— this is [the path] together with skill in means.
(a) The definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is:

the realization of all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*), which is established as the possession of qualities consisting of one hundred and seventy-three modes connected with the three types of omniscience, acquired through wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*). This is the definition.
(kha) Synonyms: the path of the bodhisattva, the path of the perfections,
the application of [knowledge of] sentient beings, the application of the knowledge of all aspects,
and the application of the knowledge of the paths.
"Practice of armor" (*sannāhapratipatti*) is synonymous with this.
(ga) As for its classification according to aspects (*ākāra*), there are one hundred and seventy-three.
From the perspective of its application, there are twenty divisions.
(gha) Regarding the limit: its boundary begins from the Mahāyāna path of accumulation (*sambhāramārga*) and extends up to the state of the Bodhisattva abiding in the final moment.
1. Regarding the aspects (*ākāra*): all the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth of the aspects have been correctly and extensively described in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* by means of five verses.
(a) The characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

The definition of the aspects (*ākāra*) is the excellence of the application consisting in cultivation, which comprises the aspects of the three types of omniscience through the inclusion of the knowledge of all modes, paths, and objects.
(b) As for their classification, there are one hundred and seventy-three distinct types of aspects.
For instance, there are twenty-seven divisions of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*),
thirty-six of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*),
and one hundred and ten of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); thus, there are one hundred and seventy-three distinct types in total.
Among the four noble truths, there are four aspects for each of the first three truths, making twelve;
and for the fourth truth, the truth of the path, there are fifteen. Thus, there are twenty-seven aspects of omniscience (or knowledge of things).
And so it is said in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*: "Beginning with the aspect of non-existence up to the form of immovability—
these four for each truth are recorded as fifteen on the path."
There are eight [aspects] of the truth of origination,
seven of the truth of the path,
and five of the truth of suffering.
And with sixteen aspects of the truth of cessation, there are thirty-six aspects of the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñatā*).
Thus it is said in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*:
"In the cause, the path, suffering, and cessation, respectively..."
They are proclaimed as eight, seven, five, and sixteen.
The thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment are the aspects of the knowledge of things (*vastujñatā*) for the Śrāvaka trainees;
there are thirty-four for the knowledge of paths (*mārgajñatā*) of the Bodhisattvas;
and there are thirty-nine unique [aspects] for the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) of the Buddhas. Thus, there are one hundred and ten aspects of the knowledge of all aspects.
And so it is said in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*:
"Beginning with the foundations of mindfulness and ending with the aspects of Buddhahood,
these are [the paths] of the disciples, the bodhisattvas, and the Buddhas, respectively."
They are considered to be thirty-seven, thirty-four, thirty, and nine,
according to the divisions of the three types of omniscience, in accordance with the Truth of the Path.
Since the forms of objects must be fully understood prior to the forms of cognition, one hundred and seventy-three forms of objects are first presented.

Second, regarding the applications (*prayoga*) and the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth of those applications, they are described in detail and with great clarity in four verses of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*.
(a) Regarding the definition:

the very cognition that consists of the absence of intrinsic nature and is free from conceptual proliferation— the nature of which is the cultivation of the union of calm abiding and insight with respect to the knower, the known, the entities, the paths, and the aspects— is here directly indicated as the definition of the application.

Alternatively—the very application (*yoga*) of sentient beings acquired here through the wisdom consisting of the cultivation of the union of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), extending from the three types of omniscience up to their aspects (*ākāra*), is the characteristic of the practice (*prayoga*) as described.
For by the phrase "due to awakening with difficulty after a long time," the practice belonging to the path of accumulation (*sambhāramārga*) is included here.
(b) The classification (*bheda*).
There are twenty varieties of applications (*prayoga*).
Among these, there are five subdivisions according to their essential nature (*svarūpa*), as follows:
the application of non-abiding due to the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) in form and the other [sense objects].
The application of non-application (*ayogaprayoga*) is because there is indeed no application regarding them;

it is the profound application (*gambhīraprayoga*) in the context of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), in the sense that the suchness of form and so forth is profound and thus no foundation is apprehended; and it is the difficult-to-penetrate application (*duravagāhaprayoga*) in the context of the knowledge of paths (*mārgajñatā*), in the sense that form and so forth are difficult to fathom because they are by nature untroubled.

Because form and so forth are immeasurable, in the sense that no limit can be apprehended, there is the "immeasurable application" within the context of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
There are eight applications based on the views regarding the person (*pudgala*).
To explain: for a beginner who is by nature prone to being terrified by profound emptiness, there is the application of attaining awakening with difficulty and after a long time.

The application for obtaining the prophecy consists in the absence of terror regarding the profound nature of phenomena from the beginning of the realization of the "heat" stage of the path of preparation, and the absence of distance from the practice of the six perfections even in dreams.
The application of non-retrogression consists in long-term cultivation concerning the domain of the realization of the nature of phenomena, beginning from the "summit" stage of clear realization.

The application of departure (*niryāṇaprayoga*) consists in the firm realization of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) through skill in means (*upāyakauśala*) beginning with patience (*kṣānti*), and in the avoidance of those factors that constitute obstacles for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

The uninterrupted application (*nirantaraprayoga*) is the certainty of being near to the direct perception of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) through the power of continuous practice—such as constant cultivation—beginning from the clear realization of the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharmābhisamaya*), because arrogance and so forth are no longer perceived; it is like being close to the great ocean.
The application for imminent awakening consists in realizing that one is the support for the causes of omniscience—the newly acquired untainted phenomena;
the application for swift awakening consists in the rapid production of the fruit, the Dharma-body;
and the application for the welfare of others consists in turning the wheel of Dharma and so forth.
There are four applications by way of the vision of the means for perfecting the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). They are as follows:

the application of neither increase nor decrease, because one is authorized to practice the perfection of wisdom by not seeing the increase or decrease of virtues and faults from the perspective of ultimate reality;
and the application of the non-apprehension of phenomena and non-phenomena, through the realization that phenomena, non-phenomena, and so forth, are ultimately unapprehendable.
Because form and so forth are of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, they are inconceivable; thus, there is the "inconceivable application.

Because they are of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, there is an absence of conceptual construction regarding form and so forth, their signs, and their intrinsic nature; thus, there is the "non-conceptual application.
These two applications are presented from the perspective of the view of the fruit of the application.

For instance, there are two [applications]: the application of bestowing the jewel of the fruit, because it bestows the jewels of the fruits beginning with stream-entry up to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; and the application of purification, because it is the cause for abandoning the obscurations of afflictions and the known.
There is one application from the perspective of swift cultivation.

Since it is the very nature of things that many obstacles arise for great jewels, therefore, even though there are many obstacles, the writing of the Mother—who is the essence of the supreme jewel—will indeed be swift within a year; such is the application of the time-limit.
3. The Qualities.
All the characteristics and so forth of the qualities (*guṇa*) have been demonstrated in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* by means of half a verse. For it is said:
